Description: The Tale of Sinuhe, the most copied prose classic of Middle Kingdom Egypt, preserved principally in two Berlin papyri: P. Berlin 3022 (Twelfth Dynasty, 311 lines, lacking the beginning) and P. Berlin 10499 (end of the Middle Kingdom, c. 1650 BC, 203 lines including the beginning), with a third major copy on a limestone ostracon in Oxford's Ashmolean Museum. It tells of Sinuhe, an official of Amenemhat I, who fled Egypt after the king's assassination, lived for years in Retenu (Canaan) under a local prince, married, raised a family, fought a champion in single combat, and finally returned to Egypt at the invitation of Senwosret I.
Interpretations: Sinuhe is fiction or semi-fiction, not history, but it is a first-rate witness to life in Canaan around 1900 BC: tribal chiefs rather than kings, pastoral wealth, wells and pastures as the prizes of war, and single combat between champions, all closely paralleling the world of the patriarchs. One scholar has suggested it as a prototype for the Joseph story (exile, prosperity abroad, reconciliation), but that is a literary comparison, not evidence of borrowing.
AlternativeNames: Tale of Sinuhe; P. Berlin 3022; P. Berlin 10499
BiblicalSignificance: It paints the Canaan that Abraham entered: a land of competing tribal chiefs, herds, wells, and desert fringes, giving the patriarchal stories a vivid contemporary backdrop.
CurrentLocation: Egyptian Museum, Berlin (P. Berlin 3022 and 10499); Ashmolean Museum, Oxford (ostracon)
